syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

topics.title: Political Theory: Its Roots and Objectives

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how reason, reflection and language form the roots of political theory.
State what political theory examines and its objective of training citizens to think rationally.
Distinguish the negative popular image of politics from politics as a worthwhile and integral activity.
Explain politics as negotiation and collective decision making at the level of government and of people.
Identify the contributions of major political thinkers to ideas such as freedom and equality.
Describe how political theory clarifies concepts and probes principles that shape constitutions and social life.

topics.title: Why Questions of Freedom and Equality Persist

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why values guaranteed formally may not be realised equally in all spheres of life.
Explain how constitutional rights are reinterpreted and expanded in response to new circumstances.
Analyse new opportunities and threats to freedom created by communication technology and the internet.
Explain why political concepts have many definitions unlike mathematical terms.
Describe how Socrates used reason to reveal the limitations of a given view of justice.
Analyse how the meaning of equality changes with context, from equal opportunity to special provisions and fair distribution.

topics.title: Why Should We Study Political Theory?

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why political theory is useful for students, professionals and voting citizens.
Evaluate how political theory helps us examine our prejudices and debate rationally.
Explain, using Nelson Mandela's struggle against apartheid, why people sacrifice for freedom.
Interpret Aung San Suu Kyi's idea that real freedom is freedom from fear.
Distinguish freedom as absence of external constraints from freedom as conditions to develop one's potential.
Explain the meaning of Swaraj as rule of the self and rule over the self, as highlighted by Tilak and Gandhi.
Identify the political, social and economic sources of constraints on freedom.
Explain why some constraints are necessary to prevent chaos and settle disputes in society.
Analyse why legal and political restraints are needed to stop one group coercively imposing its views.
Distinguish between self-regarding and other-regarding actions in J.S. Mill's harm principle.
Apply Mill's distinction between minor harm (social disapproval) and serious harm (force of law).
Explain the meaning of reasonable restrictions in Indian constitutional discussions.
Explain negative liberty as an inviolable minimum area of non-interference, or 'freedom from'.
Explain positive liberty as 'freedom to' and the enabling social conditions it requires.
State J.S. Mill's four reasons for protecting freedom of expression even for 'false' ideas.
Evaluate demands to ban books and films and the long-term effect of banning on freedom.
Explain why the capacity to make choices carries responsibility and must be built through education.
Explain equality as a moral and political ideal based on the equal worth of all human beings.
Describe the paradox that equality is widely accepted as an ideal while inequality is visible everywhere.

topics.title: What is equality? Equal opportunities and natural versus social inequalities

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why equality means equal access to basic goods and opportunities rather than identical outcomes.
Distinguish natural inequalities from socially-produced inequalities and recognise the limits of this distinction.
Identify the rights that make up political equality and explain why it is necessary but not sufficient.
Explain how social equality requires minimum conditions of life and the removal of discriminatory customs.
Explain the feminist critique of patriarchy and the distinction between sex and gender.

topics.title: Economic equality: Marxism, liberalism and socialism

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how economic inequality is measured and why entrenched inequalities are dangerous.
Compare the Marxist and liberal views on the causes of and remedies for inequality.
Describe the socialist approach to equality and Lohia's idea of Sapta Kranti.

topics.title: Formal equality and equality through differential treatment

concepts.learning_objective: Explain formal equality as the ending of legally protected privileges and discrimination.
Evaluate when differential treatment enhances rather than violates equality.

topics.title: Affirmative action and the debate on reservations

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the rationale and forms of affirmative action and its time-bound nature.
Analyse the arguments of supporters and critics of reservations as policies for equality.
Identify how different cultures and thinkers such as Plato, Confucius and ancient Indian tradition understood justice.
Explain the idea of giving each person his due and how Kant's idea of human dignity changed its meaning.
Identify the civil, political and social rights that follow from treating equals equally.
Apply the principle that people doing the same work must not be treated differently on grounds of class, caste, race or gender.
Explain why rewarding people in proportion to effort, skill and risk can be just.
Analyse why equal treatment needs to be balanced with proportionality.
Explain why taking account of special needs extends rather than contradicts equal treatment.
Evaluate the difficulty governments face in harmonising the three principles of justice.
Explain why social justice may require redistribution of resources to create a level playing field.
Identify Indian measures such as abolition of untouchability and land reforms that aim at just distribution.
Explain Rawls' idea of deciding the rules of society under a veil of ignorance.
Analyse why Rawls holds that fairness follows from rational self-interest rather than morality or generosity.
Identify the basic minimum conditions of life a just society should provide.
Evaluate when inequality makes a society unjust, given that justice does not require absolute equality.
Explain the arguments made by supporters of free markets for a just distribution.
Evaluate why the state may need to step in to provide basic facilities to the disadvantaged.
Define a right as an entitlement or justified claim and distinguish it from a mere want.
Explain dignity and well-being as grounds on which rights are claimed, and why harmful activities cannot be rights.
Describe the seventeenth and eighteenth century theory of natural rights to life, liberty and property.
Explain the idea of universal human rights and how the list of human rights has expanded.
Explain Kant's moral conception of rights based on human dignity.
Explain why legal and constitutional recognition gives rights a special status without being their basis.
Explain how rights require the state to act in some ways and to refrain from acting in others.
Identify political rights and civil liberties and explain how they make government accountable.
Distinguish economic and cultural rights and explain why democracies recognise them.
Explain the obligations that rights place on individuals, including the common good and respect for the rights of others.
Evaluate how rights are balanced when they conflict and why citizens must be vigilant about restrictions on civil liberties.
Explain citizenship as full and equal membership of a political community with rights and identity.
Recognise that citizen rights were won through historical struggles.
Describe the legal and moral obligations of citizens to each other and to society.
Analyse debates over the freedom of movement and the rights of migrant workers.
Explain how citizens can resolve disputes through protest, negotiation and courts.
Describe Martin Luther King Jr.'s arguments against segregation laws.
Examine how slum-dwellers and the urban poor struggle to exercise citizen rights.
Identify T. H. Marshall's three kinds of citizenship rights and his view of equality.
Evaluate why equal rights may require policies that respond to different needs.
Explain how nation states express national identity and its inclusiveness.
Compare the criteria for granting citizenship used in different countries.
Describe the inclusive notion of citizenship in the Indian Constitution.
Explain the problems faced by refugees and stateless people.
Analyse why the promise of universal democratic citizenship remains unfulfilled.
Explain how new communication links people across national boundaries.
Evaluate whether global citizenship could supplement or replace national citizenship.
Explain why nationalism is a powerful but hard-to-define political creed.
Identify how nationalism led both to unification of states and to the break-up of empires.
Distinguish unifying nationalism from separatist nationalist movements within existing states.

topics.title: Nation: shared beliefs, history and territory

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how a nation differs from a family or kinship group and why it is called an imagined community.
Describe how shared beliefs and a continuing historical identity constitute a nation.
Explain the significance of territory and homeland, and why it causes conflict.

topics.title: Shared political ideals and common political identity

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why a shared vision of the future and political values distinguish nations from other groups.
Evaluate why democracies should imagine the nation in political rather than cultural terms.
State the meaning of the right to national self-determination and its use by liberation movements.
Analyse the consequences of reorganising boundaries on the principle of one culture-one state.
Interpret the Basque demand for self-determination and the democratic alternative to new states.
Identify group rights given to minorities and the reinterpretation of self-determination.
Explain Rabindranath Tagore's critique of narrow nationalism.
Evaluate why an inclusive citizenship that accommodates many identities is needed in a democracy.
Explain inter-religious domination using examples of communities targeted for their religious identity.
Explain intra-religious domination and why secularism opposes it without being anti-religious.
Describe secularism as a normative doctrine promoting freedom within religions and equality between and within them.
Identify a theocratic state and explain why religious and state institutions must be separated.
Explain why separation of religion and state is necessary but not sufficient for a secular state.
Explain the western (American) idea of separation of religion and state as mutual exclusion.
Explain why the western model interprets freedom and equality individually and neglects minority rights.
Describe Kemal Ataturk's secularism of active intervention in and suppression of religion in Turkey.
Identify the differences between Indian and mainstream western secularism.
Explain how the Indian state may disengage or engage with religion, negatively or positively, in pursuit of equality.
Describe Nehru's view of secularism as equal protection to all religions and opposition to communalism.
Evaluate the criticism that secularism is anti-religious and threatens religious identity.
Evaluate the criticism that secularism is a western concept unsuited to India.
Explain, through the chapter's examples, why minority rights protect fundamental interests and are not special privileges.
Evaluate the charge that Indian secularism is interventionist, including the dilemma of personal laws.

topics.title: Criticisms: vote bank politics and impossible project

concepts.learning_objective: Analyse when vote bank politics becomes a problem for democracy and for the groups concerned.
Evaluate the claim that secularism is an impossible project and the chapter's responses to it.
